abstract: David Autor develops a framework for distinguishing genuinely new work — new tasks, roles, and industries that did not previously exist — from simple expansion of existing employment ('more work'). The key insight is that new work matters because it creates temporary expertise scarcity: workers who develop novel specialized skills command wage premiums until those skills diffuse across the labor force. This mechanism has historically been central to how labor markets absorb workers displaced by automation. Using Census and American Community Survey data from 1940-2023, Autor finds that 18% of US workers in the 2011-2023 period held jobs that were introduced since 1970. The composition of new work has shifted dramatically over time, from production and clerical roles (dominant in 1950) toward professional and managerial positions in recent decades. Technology-linked new work commands wage premiums approximately four times larger than other new work, underscoring the role of expertise scarcity in driving labor market adjustment. The paper also draws on WWII-era evidence showing that manufacturing policy created not just more jobs but genuinely new work in affected counties. The framework raises important questions about whether AI will generate new work at a pace sufficient to offset displacement, or whether it will compress the historical scarcity window that allowed workers to benefit from expertise premiums.
keyFindings: 18% of US workers (2011-2023) held jobs introduced since 1970, demonstrating the ongoing importance of new work creation
Technology-linked new work commands wage premiums approximately 4x larger than other types of new work
New work composition has shifted from production/clerical roles (1950) toward professional/managerial positions
The key distinction is expertise scarcity: new work creates temporary wage premiums that decline as skills diffuse
WWII manufacturing policy evidence shows industrial shocks can create genuinely new work, not just expand existing employment
methodology: Historical analysis using US Census and American Community Survey data from 1940-2023 to track emergence and growth of new occupational categories. Occupation-level classification of 'new work' based on when job titles first appeared in Census coding. Wage premium analysis comparing new vs. existing occupations. Quasi-experimental evidence from WWII-era county-level manufacturing policy variation.
qualifiers: Framework is primarily conceptual — does not model or predict whether AI will generate sufficient new work to offset displacement. Historical patterns of new work creation may not persist if AI automates expertise acquisition itself. The paper does not directly address AI (commenters raised this question). Measurement of 'new work' depends on Census occupation coding changes, which may lag actual emergence of new roles. US-specific data.
